title: The First Civilisations · Episode 1
chapters: Hammurabi's Code: law carved in stone

units.t: The First Civilisations. Episode one.
In this episode: Mesopotamia: where civilisation began, Hammurabi's Code: law carved in stone and The invention of writing.
Part one. Mesopotamia: where civilisation began.
Between two rivers in modern Iraq, people built the first cities, the first written laws and some of the first empires.
You still use their ideas every time you check the time.
Land between rivers.
Mesopotamia means 'land between rivers', the Tigris and Euphrates in modern Iraq.
It sat in the Fertile Crescent, an arc of good farmland from the eastern Mediterranean down to the Persian Gulf, where farming began more than 10,000 years ago with wheat, barley, sheep and goats.
The southern plain was hot and dry, and the rivers flooded unpredictably.
So people dug canals, dykes and irrigation ditches to control the water and grow a surplus.
With a surplus, not everyone had to farm, and some became priests, craftspeople, soldiers and rulers.
That shift from everyone feeding themselves to specialised jobs is the seed of civilisation.
Sumer's first cities.
In southern Mesopotamia, the Sumerians built cities such as Uruk, Ur and Lagash.
By around 3000 BC, Uruk may have held tens of thousands of people inside walls about 9 kilometres long.
Each city had its own ruler and patron god, worshipped in a temple on a stepped mud-brick platform called a ziggurat.
Cities traded grain and woollen textiles for timber, metals and stone, and fought each other over land, borders and water.
Temples and palaces owned land and herds and paid weavers, brewers and farm workers in rations of barley, bread, oil and beer.
Society was layered, from rulers and priests down to enslaved people, often war captives or debtors.
Boys from wealthier families could train for years in scribal schools.
Firsts from Sumer.
Sumerians developed cuneiform, one of the first writing systems, around 3200 BC.
They were among the first to use the wheel, first for making pottery and then for carts.
They counted in base 60, a handy number because it divides evenly by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20 and 30.
Their Babylonian successors carried it on, which is why we still have 60 seconds in a minute, 60 minutes in an hour and 360 degrees in a circle.
Sumerians also recorded the movements of the sky.
Their poems about the hero-king Gilgamesh became the Epic of Gilgamesh, one of the oldest surviving works of literature.
Empire and written law.
Around 2334 BC, Sargon rose to power.
He conquered the Sumerian cities and built the Akkadian Empire, often called the world's first, ruling many peoples from Akkad, a capital whose ruins have never been found.
Akkadian stayed the region's main written language for centuries, though the empire lasted under two centuries.
Hammurabi ruled Babylon for about 40 years.
Around 1754 BC he had 282 laws carved on a tall black stone pillar, now in the Louvre.
They covered trade, wages, loans, marriage, property, medical fees and crime.
Many followed 'an eye for an eye', but punishments depended on whether the victim was a noble, commoner or enslaved.
Its importance lay in laws being written and publicly displayed, so rules applied predictably, not at a ruler's whim.
Later empires and legacy.
In the first millennium BC, the Assyrians built a feared military empire.
From Nineveh, near modern Mosul, King Ashurbanipal gathered a great library of clay tablets, many now in the British Museum.
Nineveh fell in 612 BC, and Babylon rose again under Nebuchadnezzar II, who built huge walls and the blue-glazed Ishtar Gate, now in a Berlin museum.
The Hanging Gardens are described by later Greek writers, but no clear trace has been found.
In 539 BC, Cyrus the Great of Persia took Babylon.
Mesopotamian astronomy and mathematics influenced Greek scholars, and the flood story in Gilgamesh parallels the story of Noah.
The seven-day week may also draw on it.
Much was forgotten until archaeologists in the 1800s dug up tablets and deciphered cuneiform.
Today, looting and conflict threaten Iraqi sites.
The key idea: Controlling river water produced a farming surplus, and that surplus made specialised jobs and civilisation possible.
Part two. Hammurabi's Code: law carved in stone.
Nearly 4,000 years ago a Babylonian king had his laws carved into a towering black stone for everyone to see.
It is one of the oldest legal texts we can still read, and it is far stranger and more human than 'an eye for an eye' suggests.
A stone in the sand.
In the winter of 1901 to 1902, French archaeologists at Susa, in what is now south-western Iran, unearthed three pieces of polished black stone.
Fitted together, they formed a pillar over two metres tall, covered in tiny wedge-shaped cuneiform writing in the Akkadian language.
It was a law code issued by Hammurabi, king of Babylon, who ruled from about 1792 to 1750 BCE.
But Susa is not in Babylon.
Scholars think an Elamite king carried the stone off as war plunder in the 12th century BCE.
It now stands in the Louvre in Paris.
Hammurabi began as ruler of one city among several competing ones in Mesopotamia.
Over about four decades, diplomacy, alliances and war brought much of the south and centre under his control.
Justice from the sun god.
Running a large kingdom meant managing canals, taxes and disputes between people with different local customs.
Letters from Hammurabi's reign show a hands-on ruler, writing to officials about everything from flood repairs to a single stolen field.
His law collection, probably set up late in his reign, was meant to show that he had brought order and fairness.
At the top of the stone, a carving shows Hammurabi standing before a seated god, usually identified as Shamash, the sun god and god of justice.
A prologue lists the king's achievements, then come the laws, then an epilogue.
In it he says he set up the laws so the strong would not oppress the weak, and invites any wronged person to have the stone read to them.
Laws for everyday life.
Scholars count about 282 laws, though several columns near the bottom of the stone were deliberately rubbed away in antiquity and have been partly recovered from other copies.
Most follow a simple pattern: if someone does this, then this happens.
The subjects are surprisingly ordinary.
There are rules on renting fields and boats, interest on loans, wages for workers, fees for doctors, inheritance, divorce and the care of children.
A builder whose badly built house collapsed and killed its owner could be put to death.
A tavern keeper who cheated customers over beer could be punished.
Reading the laws is like looking through a window at the worries of ordinary Babylonians: debts, floods, unpaid bills and family quarrels.
Eye for an eye.
The code's most famous principle is retaliation: if a man destroys the eye of another man, his own eye will be destroyed.
But this applied mainly between people of the same high status.
Babylonian society had roughly three ranks: free citizens, a middle group of commoners or dependants, and enslaved people.
If a free man blinded a commoner, he paid a fine in silver instead.
If he injured an enslaved person, he paid compensation to the owner.
Women's rights depended on their family position, and some laws protected wives and widows.
The code is both fair-minded and deeply unequal, a reminder that every legal system reflects the values of its time.
Not first, not rulebook.
Hammurabi is often called the first lawgiver, but older collections survive, including one linked to Ur-Nammu of Ur, roughly three centuries earlier.
His stone stands out because it is so complete.
Historians also debate its purpose.
Thousands of Babylonian contracts and court records survive, yet they rarely cite the code.
Many scholars think it was less a statute book than a royal showcase of wise judgments for judges and scribes to learn from.
Scribes copied it for centuries.
Its big ideas still matter: laws should be written down and public, punishment should be proportionate, judges should not change decisions once made, and false accusers should be punished.
They resurface from Roman law to modern Australian courts.
The key idea: The best-known copy of Hammurabi's laws was found in Iran in 1901, far from Babylon, where it was made.
Part three. The invention of writing.
Writing was invented from scratch only a handful of times in history.
It began with accountants, not poets.
Before writing.
For most of history, knowledge passed through speech, song and memory.
People used tally marks, knotted cords and pictures, but these couldn't record language itself.
Oral cultures kept vast bodies of knowledge.
Aboriginal Australian songlines, for example, carry knowledge of country, law, navigation and seasons across many generations through song, story and dance.
Oral knowledge isn't inferior, but it depends on living people.
As farming villages grew into cities, administrators had to track taxes, trade, rations and debts across thousands of people.
In Mesopotamia, small clay tokens stood for goods such as sheep or jars of oil.
One influential theory says tokens were sealed in clay envelopes and marked outside, until people realised the marks alone would do.
Cuneiform on clay.
By around 3200 BC in Uruk, scribes drew signs for objects and numbers on clay tablets to record grain, livestock and labour.
Most of the earliest tablets are accounts and receipts.
Poems, letters, laws and stories came later, as signs came to stand for spoken words.
Scribes pressed a cut reed into damp clay, making wedge-shaped marks.
The name comes from Latin cuneus, wedge.
Pictures became abstract symbols standing for words or syllables, and learning hundreds of signs took years of schooling.
Cuneiform was adapted for Akkadian, Hittite and, in simplified form, Old Persian.
Hundreds of thousands of tablets survive, because clay lasts, especially when fires baked it hard, as when Nineveh was sacked.
Scholars in the 1800s deciphered it partly using a trilingual inscription at Behistun in Iran.
Hieroglyphs and invention.
Egyptian hieroglyphs appear around 3200 BC, about when Mesopotamian writing did, and may have developed independently.
They mixed signs for sounds and for whole ideas.
Scribes used faster scripts, hieratic and later demotic, in ink on papyrus.
After the last inscription in AD 394 the knowledge was lost.
The Rosetta Stone, found in 1799, carries one decree in hieroglyphs, demotic and Greek, and Champollion announced the decipherment in 1822.
In China, writing on animal bones and turtle shells to question ancestors dates to around 1200 BC, and modern characters descend directly from it, making it the oldest system still in use.
The Maya created a full system of several hundred signs.
Nearly every other writing system was borrowed from these few, or inspired by the idea.
The alphabet.
Early systems needed hundreds or thousands of signs, so only trained scribes could write.
Around 1800 BC, Semitic-speaking workers in Egypt and Sinai borrowed hieroglyph shapes to make a small set of signs for consonant sounds.
The Phoenicians, seafaring traders from modern Lebanon, spread their version around the Mediterranean.
It also gave rise to scripts such as Hebrew and Arabic.
The Greeks added vowels.
The Romans adapted a Greek-derived alphabet, partly via the Etruscans, into the Latin alphabet used for English today.
With only a couple of dozen letters, far more people could learn to read.
The word alphabet comes from alpha and beta.
Materials and impact.
Mesopotamians used clay, cheap and durable but heavy.
Egyptians made papyrus from Nile reeds.
Europeans later used parchment from animal skin, while early Chinese scribes wrote on bamboo strips and silk.
Paper was developed in China during the Han dynasty, about 2,000 years ago, and spread west through the Islamic world.
The Chinese also pioneered printing, and Gutenberg's press, around 1450, made books far cheaper in Europe.
Writing made history possible, which is why historians distinguish prehistory from history.
It fixed laws, enforced contracts and let knowledge build across generations.
Lists, tables and long arguments are easier on a page than in the head.
It also concentrated power, as for thousands of years only a small elite could read.
Every message you type stands on this 5,000-year-old invention.
The key idea: Writing began as bookkeeping, when growing cities needed records that didn't depend on anyone's memory.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why did irrigation help start civilisation in Mesopotamia?
Answer. It created a food surplus, so some people could do other jobs.
Question two. Why was the best-known copy of the code found in Iran rather than Babylon?
Answer. Scholars think an Elamite king took it as war plunder.
Question three. Why did writing develop as cities grew?
Answer. Administrators needed records beyond memory.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
